paragraphs.source_en: It appears that only then did my master at last understand why the detective had come to his house, and so he lowered his head and made a deep bow to the thief. This was probably because the burglar was much better-looking than the man who looked like a detective, so my master immediately mistook him for the detective. The burglar was naturally astonished, but he could hardly announce, “I am the thief,” and so he stood there as if nothing were the matter. Of course, his hands were still tucked in his sleeves. Since he was wearing handcuffs, even if he had wanted to put his hands out, he could not possibly have done so. Ordinarily, anyone would have understood the situation at a glance, but unlike most people nowadays, this master of mine has the defect of blindly revering officials and policemen. He believes that the majesty of officialdom is something exceedingly dreadful. In theory, of course, he is not unaware that policemen are merely watchmen hired with the people’s own money; but when it comes to an actual encounter, he becomes abjectly submissive. My master’s father had once been the headman of a backstreet district, and all his life he had lived bowing and scraping to those above him. That habit, by some karmic consequence, seems to have been passed down to his son. It is, indeed, most pitiful.
